claims.claim: When increasing the contribution of a rectified linear version of the predictor, the variance explained by the linear truncation drops while this is not the case for the truncation after the second-order term.
claims.source: When increasing the contribution of a rectified linear version of the predictor, the amount of variance explained by the linear truncation drops while this is not the case for the truncation after the second-order term (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: MINE increases the interpretability of the CNN model and classifies the transformations the model encapsulates according to their computational complexity.
claims.source: In summary, MINE increases the interpretability of the CNN model and classifies the transformations the model encapsulates according to their computational complexity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Receptive fields compactly describe stimulus features that drive a neuron's response.
claims.source: Receptive fields compactly describe stimulus features that drive a neuron's response (Dayan and Abbott, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Receptive fields reveal integration times and zero-crossings that indicate adapting responses.
claims.source: They reveal integration times (those times over which coefficients of the receptive field are different from zero) and zero-crossings within the receptive field signal adapting responses that indicate that a neuron encodes the derivative of a stimulus across time (e.g. velocity encoding neurons) or that it detects edges across space.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about receptive field interpretation.

claims.claim: The Taylor expansion of the CNN is equivalent to the Volterra expansion of a system processing information across time.
claims.source: Since the input to the CNN at the heart of MINE contains information about each predictor across time, the Taylor expansion introduced in the previous section (Figure 2A) is equivalent to the Volterra expansion of a system processing information across time equal to the history length of the CNN.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on the equivalence of Taylor and Volterra expansions.

claims.claim: Both MINE and directly fitting the Volterra kernels yielded receptive fields nearly indistinguishable from the ground truth when using Gaussian white noise as input.
claims.source: As expected, both MINE and directly fitting the Volterra kernels yielded receptive fields that were nearly indistinguishable from the ground truth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Under naturalistic conditions with slowly varying stimuli, MINE still yielded well-fitting receptive fields.
claims.source: Under these more naturalistic conditions, MINE still yielded well-fitting receptive fields (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: An ordinary regression fit of the Volterra kernels failed to recover the receptive fields under naturalistic conditions.
claims.source: An ordinary regression fit of the Volterra kernels, on the other hand, failed to recover the receptive fields (Figure 3B), which is in line with the observation that ANNs form an efficient route to Volterra analysis (Wray and Green, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3B and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: For high penalties, the direct fit of the Volterra kernels using Ridge regression yielded receptive fields of almost comparable quality to MINE.
claims.source: Indeed, for high penalties, the direct fit of the Volterra kernels yielded receptive fields of almost comparable quality to MINE (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The CNN model fit by MINE had slightly higher predictive power compared to the best-fit Volterra model.
claims.source: The CNN model fit by MINE also had slightly higher predictive power compared to the best-fit Volterra model as indicated by higher correlations of predicted activity on a test dataset (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: MINE is a practical solution to extract receptive fields that yields high-quality receptive fields in addition to other information about the relationship between predictors and neural responses.
claims.source: This is not to say that no other way could be found to extract the receptive fields, but it underlines the fact that MINE is a practical solution to this problem, which yields high-quality receptive fields in addition to other information about the relationship between predictors and neural responses.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The effective degrees of freedom of the CNN model are <50 despite having nearly 14,000 parameters.
claims.source: Interestingly, in spite of having nearly 14,000 parameters, the effective degrees of freedom of the CNN model are <50 and the Ridge regression models that are successful in identifying the receptive fields approach similar effective degrees of freedom (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: The effective degrees of freedom of the CNN are limited by the L1 penalty on the weights, the Dropout, and the limited number of training epochs.
claims.source: In the case of the CNN used by MINE, the effective degrees of freedom are limited by the L1 penalty on the weights (sparsity constraint), the Dropout, and the limited number of training epochs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claims.claim: MINE can recover the types of receptive fields of neurons that can be obtained with system identification approaches under a broader set of biologically relevant stimulus conditions.
claims.source: Overall these results suggest that MINE can recover the types of receptive fields of neurons that can be obtained with system identification approaches under a broader set of biologically relevant stimulus conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses in Figure 3.

claims.claim: There is a high correlation between the change in output of the Taylor expansion and the true change in network output across the ground-truth dataset.
claims.source: Across our ground-truth dataset, we find a high correlation between the change in output of the Taylor expansion and the true change in network output (Figure 4B, left panel), indicating that the local expansions using first- and second-order derivatives sufficiently capture the relationship between predictors and neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The Taylor metric correctly identifies the contributing predictors and their interactions on the ground-truth dataset.
claims.source: On our ground-truth dataset, the Taylor metric correctly identifies the contributing predictors and their interactions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claims.claim: Sorting individual terms by the Taylor metric consistently ranks those expected to contribute higher than those that should not.
claims.source: Sorting individual terms by this metric consistently ranks those that we expect to contribute (Figure 4C–E, red bars) higher than those that should not (Figure 4C–E, blue bars).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claims.claim: MINE allows for flexible analysis of the relationship between measured quantities and neural activity.
claims.source: In summary, MINE allows for flexible analysis of the relationship between measured quantities such as stimuli, behaviors, or internal states and neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the analyses throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: MINE approximates the functional form that relates predictors to neural activity and subsequently discovers this functional form.
claims.source: The flexibility comes from MINE turning analysis on its head: instead of predefining a model, MINE approximates the functional form that relates predictors to neural activity and subsequently discovers this functional form.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the MINE approach.

claims.claim: MINE does not make any assumptions about the probability distribution or functional form underlying the data it models.
claims.source: This is possible since MINE does not make any assumptions about the probability distribution or functional form underlying the data it models.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the MINE approach.

claims.claim: MINE identified more neurons than regression approaches on the zebrafish dataset.
claims.source: This allows MINE to identify more neurons than regression approaches on our zebrafish dataset (Figure 6D) while doing so in a less biased manner.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The regression approach especially failed on stimulus-driven units, leading to an overrepresentation of behavior-related activity.
claims.source: The regression approach especially failed on stimulus-driven units, leading to an overrepresentation of behavior-related activity (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The linear model identified neurons belonging to each receptive field cluster.
claims.source: Testing how many neurons in our receptive field clusters were also identified by the linear model (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) revealed that the linear model identified neurons belonging to each cluster.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: MINE increases sensitivity for identifying neurons.
claims.source: This argues that MINE increases sensitivity for identifying neurons, but at this level of analysis MINE did not necessarily identify functional types that were entirely missed by the linear model.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison data.

claims.claim: In four receptive field clusters, the linear model identified less than five neurons, meaning the cluster would have been missed entirely when using the linear model.
claims.source: However, in four clusters the linear model identified less than five neurons. This effectively means that the cluster would have been missed entirely when using the linear model data as the base for analysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Applying clustering on the neurons identified by the linear model only recovers 4 instead of the 15 unique receptive field clusters obtained with MINE.
claims.source: Accordingly, applying our clustering on the neurons identified by the linear model only recovers 4 instead of the 15 unique receptive field clusters that are obtained with MINE.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis.

claims.claim: The fit CNN models the computation of upstream or downstream circuits of the neuron in question.
claims.source: We propose that the fit CNN models the computation of upstream or downstream circuits of the neuron in question but we do not think or investigate whether it models the circuitry itself.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the interpretation of the CNN.

claims.claim: Given the simplicity of the CNN used in MINE, it is unlikely to provide interesting details about the circuitry itself.
claims.source: This could be investigated in the future, but given the simplicity of the CNN used in MINE it is unlikely to provide interesting details in this manner.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of the approach.

claims.claim: MINE applied to the mouse cortical dataset identified >91% of all components per session on average.
claims.source: On average, this led to the identification of >91% of all components per session (Figure 5C) on which Taylor metric and complexity were computed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: MINE assigns low complexity to the majority of cortical components; only 3% of fit components have a linear approximation score <0.8.
claims.source: Notably, MINE assigns low complexity to the majority of components; only 3% of fit components have a linear approximation score <0.8.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The relationships between predictors and neural activity in the cortical dataset are largely linear.
claims.source: This means that the relationships between predictors and neural activity are largely linear (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The apparent linearity in the cortical dataset is likely caused by the low resolution of the data, where each component blends the activity of hundreds of thousands of neurons.
claims.source: While this may seem surprising given the high nonlinearity of cortical processing, it is likely caused by the low resolution of the data. Each component blends the activity of hundreds of thousands of neurons. Averaging across many individual neurons that each may have their own nonlinear responses likely obfuscates nonlinear effects.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed linearity.

claims.claim: Visual stimuli contribute most strongly to responses in visual cortical areas with the expected left-right asymmetry.
claims.source: Specifically, visual stimuli are shown to contribute most strongly to responses in visual cortical areas with the expected left–right asymmetry (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Taylor metric mapping shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Cortical regions enhanced for whisking correspond very well to regions marked strongly with a whisk event kernel in Musall et al., 2019a.
claims.source: At the same time, comparing visual sensory responses to whisk responses shows that cortical regions enhanced for whisking (Figure 5G) correspond very well to regions marked strongly with a whisk event kernel in Figure 2 of Musall et al., 2019a.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Taylor metric mapping shown in Figure 5G and comparison to published data.

claims.claim: Instructed left and right grab events largely contribute to motor cortical regions with the expected left-right asymmetry.
claims.source: Furthermore, instructed left and right grab events largely contribute to motor cortical regions, again with the expected left–right asymmetry (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Taylor metric mapping shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Receptive fields for left and right visual stimuli in contralateral brain regions are highly similar to each other.
claims.source: Receptive fields for left and right visual stimuli in contralateral brain regions are highly similar to each other (Figure 5I, left).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the receptive field clustering shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: The excitatory effect in visual receptive fields is stronger than the inhibitory effect.
claims.source: The excitatory effect is stronger than the inhibitory effect (larger coefficients in the positive receptive fields) and both are clearly biphasic.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: The biphasic structure of visual receptive fields mimics the linear regression kernel in Musall et al., 2019a.
claims.source: We note that this biphasic structure mimics the linear regression kernel in Figure 3b of Musall et al., 2019a.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to published data.

claims.claim: Visual receptive fields have essentially zero weight after the current time, which is expected since future stimuli are unlikely to influence current neural activity.
claims.source: The visual receptive fields have essentially zero weight after the current time, which is expected since future stimuli are unlikely to influence current neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data with a logical explanation.

claims.claim: The receptive fields of left and right grab neurons are much sharper than visual receptive fields, indicating that these neurons influence movement over short timescales.
claims.source: The receptive fields of left and right grab neurons, on the other hand, are much sharper, indicating that these neurons influence movement over short timescales (Figure 5I, right).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: Grab-related receptive fields contain coefficients different from baseline for up to 100 ms into the future, suggesting preparatory activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, the grab-related receptive fields contain coefficients different from baseline for up to 100 ms into the future. This suggests preparatory activity, that is, that future movements are reflected in current neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: Temporal transformations of stimuli are a notable feature of how zebrafish process temperature information.
claims.source: Temporal transformations of stimuli are a notable feature of how zebrafish process temperature information.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Neurons that compute the rate of change of the temperature stimulus have been identified in larval zebrafish.
claims.source: In previous research, we identified neurons and centers in the larval zebrafish brain that process temperature: specifically, neurons that compute the rate of change of the temperature stimulus (Haesemeyer et al., 2018) as well as neurons whose activity is consistent with integration of temperature fluctuations (Haesemeyer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Neurons whose activity is consistent with integration of temperature fluctuations have been identified in larval zebrafish.
claims.source: In previous research, we identified neurons and centers in the larval zebrafish brain that process temperature: specifically, neurons that compute the rate of change of the temperature stimulus (Haesemeyer et al., 2018) as well as neurons whose activity is consistent with integration of temperature fluctuations (Haesemeyer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Simple regression-based approaches failed to identify neurons involved in temperature processing due to the nature of temporal transformations.
claims.source: Due to the nature of these transformations, which were unknown a priori, simple regression-based approaches failed to identify neurons involved in temperature processing.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous approaches.

claims.claim: Clustering was previously used to identify temperature processing neurons but precluded identifying neurons that integrate thermosensory stimuli and behavioral actions.
claims.source: We therefore previously resorted to clustering to identify these neurons. However, because behavior is stochastic, one particular drawback of clustering was that it precluded identifying neurons that integrate thermosensory stimuli and behavioral actions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous approaches.

claims.claim: A total of 750 planes across 25 larval zebrafish were imaged, providing slightly more than fourfold coverage of the larval zebrafish brain.
claims.source: We imaged a total of 750 planes across 25 larval zebrafish that expressed the nuclear calcium indicator H2B:GCaMP6s Freeman et al., 2014 in all neurons and the excitatory neuron marker vglut2a-mCherry Satou et al., 2013 in presumed glutamatergic neurons. This dataset provided slightly more than fourfold coverage of the larval zebrafish brain.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental dataset.

claims.claim: 40% of the identified neurons were exclusively identified by MINE, indicating the superiority of the model-discovery approach.
claims.source: 40% of these neurons, however, were exclusively identified by MINE (Figure 6D), indicating the superiority of the model-discovery approach.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: MINE consistently identifies more neurons regardless of the cutoff imposed on test data.
claims.source: In fact, MINE consistently identifies more neurons regardless of the cutoff imposed on test data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: A total of 33 functional neuron classes were identified, all of which were identified across multiple fish.
claims.source: In total, we identified 33 functional neuron classes all of which were identified across multiple fish (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The vast majority of reticulospinal neurons were classified by MINE to be driven by behavioral features.
claims.source: As a control, we labeled reticulospinal neurons in six fish via spinal backfills and as expected the vast majority of these neurons were classified by MINE to be driven by behavioral features (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the control data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Multiple functional classes of neurons with mixed selectivity were identified across the brain.
claims.source: Across the brain, we identified multiple functional classes of neurons with mixed selectivity, that is, neurons with activity jointly driven by the temperature stimulus and behavioral outputs (Figure 6E, blue filled bars).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Mixed-selectivity neurons mark a previously unidentified class of neurons in the thermoregulatory circuit that might play a key role in behavioral thermoregulation.
claims.source: These mark a previously unidentified class of neurons in the thermoregulatory circuit that might play a key role in behavioral thermoregulation: they could allow the animal to relate behavioral output to temperature changes and thereby characterize the thermal landscape.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of the identified neurons.

claims.claim: Stimulus-, Behavior- and Mixed-selectivity neurons are generally broadly distributed but enriched in specific brain regions.
claims.source: While Stimulus-, Behavior- and Mixed-selectivity neurons are generally broadly distributed, they are enriched in specific brain regions (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-I.

claims.claim: Stimulus-driven neurons are enriched in telencephalic regions, as well as the habenula and its output region the interpeduncular nucleus.
claims.source: We found stimulus-driven neurons to be enriched in telencephalic regions, as well as the habenula and its output region the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Behavior-driven neurons are enriched in hindbrain regions and the midbrain nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
claims.source: As expected, behavior-driven neurons are enriched in hindbrain regions and the midbrain nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H; Severi et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H and citations.

claims.claim: Mixed-selectivity neurons are strongly enriched in the raphe superior as well as the caudal hypothalamus and the torus longitudinalis.
claims.source: Mixed-selectivity neurons occupy some regions shared with stimulus-driven neurons such as telencephalic area M4 and the interpeduncular nucleus but are also strongly enriched in the raphe superior as well as the caudal hypothalamus and the torus longitudinalis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: Temperature-sensitive neurons were found in a medial zone of the olfactory epithelium.
claims.source: Our current dataset did not cover sensory ganglia well (especially not the trigeminal ganglion) with the exception of the olfactory epithelium where we found temperature-sensitive neurons in a medial zone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The finding of temperature-sensitive neurons in the olfactory epithelium is in line with reports in mice and frogs.
claims.source: This is in line with reports in mice and frogs that describe specific thermosensitive neurons in the olfactory epithelium of these species (Schmid et al., 2010; Kludt et al., 2015; Fleischer, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies in other species.

claims.claim: Functional cell types identified by MINE segregate spatially within the brain, likely forming organizational units within the thermoregulatory circuit.
claims.source: Overall these results demonstrate that functional cell types identified by MINE segregate spatially within the brain, likely forming organizational units within the thermoregulatory circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the anatomical analyses.

claims.claim: Analyzing brain regions for enrichment of encoding different behavioral features suggests a segregation in the control of swim starts, swim speed (vigor), and turn angle (directionality).
claims.source: Analyzing brain regions for enrichment of encoding different behavioral features suggests a segregation in the control of swim starts, swim speed (vigor), and turn angle (directionality).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: Swim start neurons are enriched in the dorsal thalamus as well as the medial hindbrain.
claims.source: Swim start neurons are enriched in the dorsal thalamus as well as the medial hindbrain, while the ventral thalamus, the forebrain, and the locus coeruleus preferentially encode swim speed (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The ventral thalamus, the forebrain, and the locus coeruleus preferentially encode swim speed.
claims.source: Swim start neurons are enriched in the dorsal thalamus as well as the medial hindbrain, while the ventral thalamus, the forebrain, and the locus coeruleus preferentially encode swim speed (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Neurons that encode turning are enriched in mid- and hindbrain regions.
claims.source: Neurons that encode turning are enriched in mid- and hindbrain regions (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Neurons encoding behavioral features could be involved in controlling these features or alternatively maintain efference copies of the motor commands for other purposes.
claims.source: Notably, these neurons could be involved in controlling these behavioral features or alternatively maintain efference copies of the motor commands for other purposes (Odstrcil et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of the neurons, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Clustering of temperature encoding neurons according to receptive fields resulted in 15 clusters, with neurons from at least 15 fish in each cluster.
claims.source: A clustering approach based on the cosine similarity of receptive fields (see 'Methods') resulted in 15 clusters. For each of these clusters, neurons came from at least 15 fish across our dataset.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Each receptive field cluster represents a functional neuron class that extracts specific features of the temperature stimulus.
claims.source: Each cluster represents a functional neuron class that extracts specific features of the temperature stimulus (Figure 7B, left).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Clusters 1 and 4 are enriched in the forebrain and are most responsive to heating and cooling stimuli over slow timescales, respectively.
claims.source: Clusters 1 and 4 are enriched in the forebrain (Figure 7B, right), and their receptive fields suggest that they are most responsive to heating and cooling stimuli over slow timescales, respectively (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and receptive field analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: Cluster 3 computes the rate of heating over shorter timescales and is almost exclusively localized to the hindbrain.
claims.source: Cluster 3, on the other hand, computes the rate of heating over shorter timescales (Figure 7C) and is almost exclusively localized to the hindbrain (Figure 7B, right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and receptive field analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: Cluster 12 represents neurons that are excited by colder temperatures and is found predominantly in hind- and midbrain regions.
claims.source: Cluster 12 represents neurons that are excited by colder temperatures since the receptive field exclusively has negative coefficients (Figure 7C). This neuron type is found predominantly in hind- and midbrain regions (Figure 7B, right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical and receptive field analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: Some receptive fields have the largest departures from 0 at the start and end, which might indicate that the chosen history length (10 s) is too short.
claims.source: We note that some of the uncovered receptive fields (e.g. clusters 1 and 4) have the largest departures from 0 at the start and end of the receptive fields. This might indicate that the chosen history length (here 10  s) is too short and does not cover the entire timescale of processing, which could be a result of the rather slow nuclear calcium indicator we chose for this study.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential limitation of the analysis.

claims.claim: Mixed-selectivity neurons could provide zebrafish with important information about the thermal environment such as the slope of temperature gradients.
claims.source: Mixed-selectivity neurons could provide zebrafish with important information about the thermal environment such as the slope of temperature gradients the fish can use to thermoregulate.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of mixed-selectivity neurons.

claims.claim: Clustering of nonlinear mixed-selectivity neurons according to response landscapes revealed diverse modes of integration across 10 clusters.
claims.source: Clustering neurons according to these response landscapes (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) revealed diverse modes of integration across 10 clusters.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Some mixed-selectivity neurons appear to add behavioral inputs linearly with thermosensory inputs.
claims.source: Some neurons appear to add behavioral inputs linearly with thermosensory inputs (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, clusters 8 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the response landscape analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Some mixed-selectivity neurons show gating, where swim drive effectively scales the sensory responsiveness.
claims.source: Other neurons, however, show gating (Figure 7D, left, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, clusters 0 and 1). Here swim drive effectively scales the sensory responsiveness.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the response landscape analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Gating neurons could act as coincidence detectors that inform larval zebrafish that temperature changes are linked to behavior as expected in a temperature gradient.
claims.source: These neurons could therefore act as coincidence detectors that inform larval zebrafish that temperature changes are linked to behavior as expected in a temperature gradient.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of gating neurons.

claims.claim: A cluster of neurons displays complex integration of sensory and motor information, with asymmetric response to temperature depending on swim drive.
claims.source: We also found a cluster of neurons that display more complex integration of sensory and motor information (Figure 7D, right). At lower-than-average swim drive, these neurons symmetrically respond to both low and high sensory drive. However, at high swim drive, the response to positive sensory drive is enhanced, making the response of the neuron to temperature asymmetric in this regime.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the response landscape analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Complexity is mapped onto both functional and anatomical features, indicating that this division is meaningful.
claims.source: We found that complexity is mapped onto both functional (Figure 7E) and anatomical features (Figure 7F), indicating that this division is not arbitrary but rather indicates a meaningful difference in neuron function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the complexity analysis shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claims.claim: Three receptive field clusters have lower complexity than expected, indicating that most neurons in these clusters have responses that linearly depend on the temperature stimulus.
claims.source: Specifically, averaging the complexity score for different receptive field clusters reveals that three of these clusters have lower complexity than expected, indicating that most neurons in these clusters have responses that linearly depend on the temperature stimulus (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the complexity analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Cluster 6 had an average complexity score >1, indicating that the majority of neurons in this cluster compute highly nonlinear transformations of the stimulus.
claims.source: One cluster (cluster 6) had an average complexity score >1, indicating that the majority of neurons in this cluster compute highly nonlinear transformations of the stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the complexity analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Within the hindbrain, neurons of complexity class 2 are found medially in rhombomeres 1 and 2.
claims.source: Within the hindbrain, neurons of complexity class 2 are found medially in rhombomeres 1 and 2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical clustering shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Neurons in the medial hindbrain region carry little information about ongoing behavior, which might indicate that they process thermosensory stimuli for other functions.
claims.source: We previously found that neurons in this region carry little information about ongoing behavior, which might indicate that they process thermosensory stimuli for other functions (Haesemeyer et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is a speculative statement.

claims.claim: Prominent clusters of complexity 2 neurons can be found in the habenula and dorsal telencephalon, consistent with the idea that these structures are involved in higher-order computations.
claims.source: Prominent clusters of complexity 2 neurons can also be found in the habenula and dorsal telencephalon consistent with the idea that these structures are involved in higher-order computations rather than the short-time control of thermoregulatory behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical clustering shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Linear neurons are enriched in the posterior and medial hindbrain.
claims.source: Linear neurons, on the other hand, are enriched in the posterior and medial hindbrain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the anatomical clustering shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: MINE has the potential to greatly aid the analysis of large-scale neural data.
claims.source: In summary, these data reveal the power of MINE to identify computational features leading to a detailed classification of neurons into functional types. This automated, unbiased, and highly flexible analysis framework has the potential to greatly aid the analysis of large-scale neural data.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the results throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: MINE functionality is exposed through a simple Python interface.
claims.source: To facilitate the adoption of MINE, we expose its functionality through a simple Python interface.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the software implementation.

results.result: MINE is a computational framework that uses a three-layer CNN architecture with a linear convolutional layer and two dense layers with continuously differentiable activation functions (swish) to model relationships between predictors and neural activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C18, C33-C38 describe the MINE architecture and design choices, supported by Figure 1A and methodological descriptions. The architecture is simple, uses specific activation functions to enable derivative calculations, and hyperparameters were optimized on test data. These design choices are well-documented and justified.

results.result: MINE uses Taylor expansion to characterize computational complexity of neural transformations, classifying neurons into complexity classes (0, 1, 2) based on whether linear, quadratic, or higher-order terms are needed to explain neural activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C20-C22, C53-C54, C57-C59, C61, C63, C66 describe the Taylor decomposition approach for complexity analysis, supported by Figure 2 and ground-truth validation. ROC analysis (C2E) shows 99% accuracy in distinguishing linear from nonlinear transformations with acceptable false-positive/negative rates at R²<0.8 threshold.

results.result: MINE extracts neural receptive fields through Taylor expansion equivalence to Volterra kernels, performing comparably or better than direct Volterra fitting under naturalistic stimulus conditions while maintaining low effective degrees of freedom (<50 despite ~14,000 parameters).
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C67-C80 describe receptive field extraction, supported by Figure 3 simulations. MINE matches direct Volterra fitting with white noise (C72) and outperforms ordinary regression under naturalistic conditions (C73-C74). Ridge regression with high penalties approaches MINE performance (C75), but MINE shows slightly higher predictive power (C76) and maintains low effective degrees of freedom through regularization (C78-C79).

results.result: MINE identifies which predictors and their interactions drive neural responses through Taylor decomposition, correctly ranking contributing predictors on ground-truth data without making assumptions about probability distributions or functional forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C82-C87 describe predictor identification via Taylor metrics, supported by Figure 4. High correlation between Taylor expansion and true network output (C82, Figure 4B) validates the approach. The method correctly identifies contributing predictors and interactions on ground-truth data (C83-C84, Figure 4C-E), demonstrating the model-free flexibility of the approach.

results.result: On ground-truth data, MINE identifies responses dependent on predictors regardless of linearity, learns temporal transformations (shifts, convolutions, derivatives), and outperforms simple linear regression while matching expanded linear models with interaction terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C40-C42, C44-C47 describe ground-truth validation, supported by Figure 1. Simple linear regression fails (C40, Figure 1F), while expanded linear models with interaction terms match CNN performance in some categories (C42). MINE's advantage is learning temporal transformations without explicit predictor augmentation (C45-C47), removing the need for a priori calcium kernel estimation.

results.result: MINE applied to mouse cortical widefield imaging data identified >91% of components, revealed largely linear relationships (only 3% with linear score <0.8), and recovered expected anatomical organization of sensory and motor responses with biologically plausible receptive field structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C96-C109 describe cortical data analysis, supported by Figure 5. High identification rate (C96), low complexity (C97-C98), and anatomically appropriate Taylor metric mappings (C100-C102) validate the method. The observed linearity (C98) is explained by low spatial resolution averaging across many neurons (C99). Receptive field analysis shows expected temporal structure for sensory (past-weighted) and motor (preparatory) responses (C103-C109).

results.result: In zebrafish thermoregulatory circuits, MINE identified 42,229 neurons (40% exclusively by MINE) across 33 functional classes, including a novel class of mixed-selectivity neurons integrating thermosensory and behavioral information that traditional methods failed to identify.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31, C6-C9, C88-C89, C115, C118-C122 describe zebrafish experiments, supported by Figures 6-7. MINE identified significantly more neurons than linear regression (C88, C118-C119, Figure 6D), with less bias toward behavior-related activity (C89). The 33 functional classes were reproducible across fish (C120), and reticulospinal control validates behavioral classification (C121). Mixed-selectivity neurons represent a novel discovery (C8, C31, C122).

results.result: Functional neuron types identified by MINE in zebrafish show anatomical segregation, with stimulus-driven neurons enriched in telencephalon and habenula, behavior-driven neurons in hindbrain, and mixed-selectivity neurons in raphe superior, caudal hypothalamus, and torus longitudinalis.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C130, C32 describe anatomical organization, supported by Figure 6H and supplements. Anatomical clustering and Z-Brain registration reveal spatial segregation of functional types (C124, C130). Specific enrichments are documented for each type (C125-C127), including temperature-sensitive neurons in olfactory epithelium consistent with other species (C128-C129). The anatomical mapping validates functional classifications.

results.result: Receptive field clustering of zebrafish temperature-encoding neurons revealed 15 functional classes with distinct temporal processing characteristics and anatomical distributions, including neurons computing heating/cooling rates over different timescales and neurons responding to absolute temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C141 describe receptive field analysis, supported by Figure 7A-C. Behavioral feature encoding shows anatomical segregation (C131-C134). Receptive field clustering identified 15 reproducible classes (C136-C137) with interpretable temporal characteristics (C138-C140). The observation that some receptive fields peak at boundaries (C141) is acknowledged as a potential limitation of the 10s history length.

results.result: Mixed-selectivity neurons in zebrafish show diverse integration modes across 10 clusters, including linear addition, gating (where swim drive scales sensory responsiveness), and complex asymmetric integration of thermosensory and behavioral information.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 describe mixed-selectivity neuron analysis, supported by Figure 7D. Response landscape clustering revealed 10 distinct integration modes (C143), including linear addition (C144), gating (C145), and complex asymmetric responses (C147). The gating neurons are interpreted as potential coincidence detectors (C146), though this functional interpretation is speculative. The diversity of integration modes is well-documented.

results.result: Computational complexity in zebrafish maps onto both functional and anatomical features, with linear neurons enriched in posterior/medial hindbrain and complexity-2 neurons in habenula, dorsal telencephalon, and medial hindbrain rhombomeres 1-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C154 describe complexity mapping, supported by Figure 7E-F. Complexity varies across receptive field clusters (C149-C150) and shows anatomical organization (C151, C153-C154). The interpretation that complexity-2 neurons in habenula/telencephalon perform higher-order computations (C153) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The citation to prior work (C152) supports the functional interpretation of medial hindbrain neurons.

results.result: Comparison to linear models shows MINE increases sensitivity for neuron identification, with four receptive field clusters containing <5 neurons identified by linear regression, resulting in only 4 of 15 clusters being recoverable using linear model data.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 describe linear model comparison, supported by Figure 7 and supplements. While linear models identified neurons in each cluster (C90), MINE showed higher sensitivity (C91). Four clusters were essentially missed by linear regression (C92), and clustering on linear model data recovered only 4/15 clusters (C93). This demonstrates MINE's advantage in identifying functional types, not just individual neurons.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the motivation for MINE by noting that brains evolved rather than being engineered, making it unclear how well predefined models capture neural activity, while ANNs offer flexibility but are difficult to interpret.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C17 establish background and motivation, supported by appropriate citations. The evolutionary argument (C1) and uncertainty about model choice (C2) motivate the model-free approach. The review of linear regression (C12-C13) and ANNs (C14-C17) is accurate and well-cited. This provides solid conceptual foundation for MINE.

results.result: MINE inverts the usual analysis approach by discovering functional forms from data rather than predefining them, though the CNN architecture and hyperparameters impose some limits on modelable relationships.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C23-C26 describe MINE's conceptual approach. The 'model-free' characterization (C26) is qualified by acknowledging architectural constraints (C25). The convolutional layer's ability to learn temporal transformations (C23-C24) is a reasonable inference based on CNN properties. The conceptual framing is accurate and appropriately nuanced.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that while nonlinear computation is believed to underlie nervous system function, many neurons show nearly linear responses to sensory/behavioral features, aligning with the hypothesis that important information should be linearly decodable.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 establish background on linearity/nonlinearity, supported by appropriate citations. The tension between nonlinear computation (C48-C49) and observed linear responses (C50-C51) motivates the complexity analysis. The inference that disambiguating linear/nonlinear processing provides circuit insight (C52) is reasonable. This provides good motivation for the complexity metric.

results.result: Previous work identified neurons computing temperature rate-of-change and integration in zebrafish, but simple regression failed due to unknown temporal transformations, and clustering precluded identifying neurons integrating thermosensory and behavioral information.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 describe prior work limitations, supported by self-citations. The statements about previous findings (C110-C112) and methodological limitations (C113-C114) provide context for why MINE was needed for the zebrafish experiments. This appropriately motivates the application.

results.result: The authors propose that the CNN models computations of upstream/downstream circuits but acknowledge that the simple CNN architecture is unlikely to provide detailed circuit-level insights.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are explicit speculative statements about CNN interpretation. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and do not overclaim about circuit modeling. This represents appropriate scientific caution about what the method can and cannot reveal.

results.result: MINE has potential to aid large-scale neural data analysis and is made accessible through a simple Python interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C156 are summary statements about MINE's utility and accessibility. The potential for aiding analysis (C155) is supported by the demonstrated results throughout the manuscript. The Python interface (C156) is documented in Table 1. These are appropriate concluding statements.
